Saved. This question exposed generalizable patterns worth keeping for future Treasury Bulletin questions:

What I captured (skill `officeqa-treasury-bulletin` + one memory entry):

1. Table location — ESF questions come from the Balance Sheet section; "last day of March 1989" = the March 31, 1989 dated column, and balance sheets show two dated columns so picking the right one matters.

2. Units/scaling — ESF figures print in thousands of dollars; questions want billions, so divide by 1,000,000. Confirm the unit header before scaling.

3. Balance-sheet identities (the reusable insight) — Total assets = Total liabilities and capital; "Total capital" is a subtotal while "Total liabilities and capital" is the grand total, so their absolute difference equals Total liabilities. That's a built-in cross-check for any future capital/liabilities/assets arithmetic.

4. Output/parsing discipline — `[v1, v2]` in sub-question order, units and rounding applied to every value, and re-reading which quantities are actually requested vs. merely used to define an operation.

The verdict was correct, but the structural facts (units convention, balance-sheet identity, column-selection gotcha) recur across Treasury Bulletin questions, so they earned their place.
